title: Good feelings
hookLine: the Stoics kept joy, wise wishing and caution
last: PRIMUS MOTUS — THE JOLT ISN'T ME.

cards: After a week on the porch, you might picture the Stoic with the joy dialed down to zero. Character is the only good. Comforts are just preferred.
Feelings have judgments hiding in them. Check the jolt before you agree. It can sound like a person who never laughs at a wedding.
But the Stoics had a word for the feelings they wanted more of. Not fewer feelings. Better ones.

teach.b: Eupatheia is Greek: eu, good or well, plus pathos, the word we met two days ago. Good feelings. Diogenes Laërtius reports that the Stoics named three, each the healthy twin of a passion.
Instead of giddy, grasping pleasure, joy: a calm, deep gladness at what's truly good.
Instead of craving, wishing: wanting something wisely, in the right measure. Instead of fear, caution: sensible care about real dangers, like looking both ways without panicking about the traffic.
The same report lists finer kinds under each: under wishing, goodwill and warm affection; under joy, delight and cheerfulness. Notice: three twins for four passions.

There's no good version of distress for the fully wise person, because the Stoics thought such a person had nothing truly bad to grieve over. That's one of their hardest claims, and i'll be honest about it in two weeks.

teach.h: REAL JOY IS A SERIOUS THING.
teach.b: Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, says, roughly, believe me, real joy is a serious thing. Not a sugar rush: steady, from inside, and it doesn't vanish when the party ends.
So look back at this week. Home to the porch. Arete, character first.
The four virtues. Adiaphora, nice not needed. Pathos, and the sentence inside a feeling.
Primus motus. And now the good feelings. The goal was never a cold life.
It was a clear one, with room for gladness no one can take.

how: Modern Stoic practitioners distinguish calm joy from excited pleasure and caution from fear, and try to cultivate the steady versions.

o: a calm with no feelings at all, good or bad
a warm sympathy for other people's suffering
good feelings: calm joy, wise wishing and caution

s: the Stoics wanted a life without feeling
they wanted better feelings: joy, wise wishing, caution.
eupatheia joins eu, good, and pathos
good feelings, the healthy twins of the passions.
the Stoics named a good version of every passion
three twins for four passions; distress has none for the wise.

games.q: a Stoic sees a car coming as she steps off the curb. which good feeling fits?
games.why: caution is the healthy twin of fear: sensible care about a real danger, without panic.

practice: Find one good feeling that's here right now, or was here today: gladness at the light, relief, warmth for someone, the quiet satisfaction of a task done. Let it be exactly as big as it is, not inflated, not waved away.

wordCard.voice: Eupatheia. Greek for good feelings: joy, wise wishing and caution, the healthy twins of the passions.

orig.note: Greek: good feeling; eu, well, plus pathos, feeling.

carryVoice: Your line: joy is allowed. That's the week back on the porch; next week, the Stoic world. Day two hundred eighty-seven, done.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
